motivation: In 1979 Tajima (with the late John Dawson) proposed that an intense laser pulse driving a plasma wake could accelerate electrons with fields thousands of times stronger than those in conventional radio-frequency cavities. This was an elegant result of collective plasma theory, and it made a concrete, testable prediction. Over the next 25 years, experiments led by Malka and Leemans, among others, turned the idea into reality. In 2004 they produced quasi-monoenergetic GeV-class electron beams over millimetre-to-centimetre distances, later reaching multi-GeV energies, and drove compact X-ray and betatron sources. Laser wakefield acceleration has created a new branch of accelerator physics. It opens the way to table-top light sources and future colliders, and it gives access to the strong-field regime where radiation reaction and QED effects in plasmas can be studied. The discovery joins deep plasma theory with transformative experimental capability.
